newsitem.title: USA: Clinton was urged to reward fund-raisers. [CORRECTED 00:23 GMT 15/04]
newsitem.headline: Clinton was urged to reward fund-raisers. [CORRECTED 00:23 GMT 15/04]

text.p: A month after he was elected president in 1992, Bill Clinton was urged to consider giving jobs in his administration to people who had helped raise funds for his campaign, according to papers released by the Democratic Party on Monday.

The papers, which were among about 10,000 documents subpoenaed by a House committee investigating fund-raising abuses in the 1996 campaign, showed that fund-raisers for the Democrats were given top priority status in recommendations for jobs in the new administration.

"We urge you to consider strongly the following leading national fund-raisers who are interested in serving in the White House," party officials (corrects source of letter from co-chairman Donald Fowler) said in a letter to a coordinator for administration jobs.
"We are pleased to sponsor these 'must considers'," he added.
Among those listed for future jobs was John Huang, a central figure in current investigations of potential campaign fund-raising abuses by Clinton's party.
Huang did not get the sub-cabinet post he sought, but instead got a lower-level job in the Commerce Department as a deputy assistant secretary in the international trade area.
Before that, Huang, a naturalised American citizen who was born in China, was a top official of the Lippo Group, an international financial conglomerate based in Indonesia.

He joined the Democratic National Committee (DNC) as a vice chairman of finance in early 1996 and raised $3 million -- but party officials returned much of his solicited money as an improper or illegal foreign donation.
He left the DNC in November 1996 after allegations surfaced about fund-raising abuses in the campaign.

Others on the list of fund-raisers recommended for administration jobs included Arthur Levitt, who became chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission but has not been linked with the current fund-raising dispute.
